# Parosahassajātaka (Ja 99)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Parosahassajātaka* (Ja 99) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon. According to the canonical verse and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the story opens with the moral that a single wise person who understands the meaning of what is spoken is superior to more than a thousand fools (*parosahassa*) [Fausböll 1877]. The frame story notes that the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana concerning a question regarding ordinary or unconverted people (*puthujjanapucchaka*), an incident also associated with the *Sarabhaṅgajātaka* [Fausböll 1877]. In the Dhammapada commentary, the Buddha relates this jātaka following his descent from Tāvatiṃsa heaven upon questioning his disciples and praising the wisdom of Sāriputta [Burlingame 1921].

In the past-life narrative, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic master who had attained the formless meditative attainments; upon his deathbed, he stated that he had attained "nothing" (referring to the sphere of nothingness), which his obtuse fellow hermits misconstrued as an admission of meditative failure until the Bodhisatta descended from the Brahmā realm to correct their misunderstanding [Shaw 2006; Fausböll 1877]. In the *samodhāna*, the chief disciple is identified as Sāriputta and the Mahābrahmā as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877]. The immediately following story, the *Parosatajātaka* (Ja 100), is structurally and textually identical in background, exposition, and identification, differing primarily by substituting a single word in the opening stanza [Fausböll 1877], a relationship also reflected in Pagan-period temple epigraphy where Ja 100 is designated as *Dutiya Parosahassa* [WinThanTun 2002].
